text: ​ @KevinLindsay1  I think you have misunderstood the issue first of all, he has a view and just because Nvidia or some of his viewers do not agree that is not a good reason to not send cards. I turned off Ray Tracing in Cyberpunk 2077 as did not feel the benefit compared to the extra frames by having it off.   I do feel DLSS is a feature he glossed over in this particular video but as he says support is so limited for it at the moment.  Also no point talking about what may be supported in the future as AMD will probably have a DLSS type feature in the future, if we speculate about what feature games or drivers may may support I feel that would be bias.  On Cyberpunk I would not use DLSS it if the game was not so poorly optimised, even on quality setting I find thinks look noticeably worse in some places however even with a 2080ti at 1440p (UW screen) I need to use it to get a good frame rate even without ray tracing.  Reviewers should have no obligation to agree with product providers about what features are important, that is the whole idea of having independent reviews.  Yes he was surprised they decided not to send him more, as were every independent reviewer and most viewers.  I was planning to buy an NVidia card (indeed I bought a 2080ti) but after seeing there willingness to send out an email like that I am having seconds thoughts on if I am willing to support them as a company.   That is not bias as you would call it but rather despite thinking ray tracing and DLSS currently gives Nvidia the edge I just choose not to support a company with employees that would support such questionable business practices.  Having an view about what is important is not bias, or at least if it is then everyone is bias.  Now if he had AMD stock or Nvidia stock that could make him bias in his review but believing ray tracing a DLSS is not a feature worth worrying about at the moment, from what I have seen I sort of agree. It's because amd didn't wanna make a faster card than the 5700xt. author: @Hardwareunboxed

text:
​ @Hardwareunboxed  I'm sorry but you're drawing conclusions that are not supported by the data.

RT is not 'meh' on both. RT is actually usable on nvidia, The performance hit is much much greater on AMD to the point where enabling RT makes most games that support it unplayable. The visual improvement is subjective, but I think most people will agree that ray tracing properly implemented looks stunning and is one of the best new graphical technologies in games for years. I agree there are a limited number of games that support it currently, but you're choosing to ignore that number is growing quickly. The same applies to DLSS.

SAM only has any meaningful impact in a very limited number of games. Unsurprisingly, these are the games AMD chose to show during its announcement and are also the games you have chosen to show here. Test another 10 games and prove me wrong.

At the end of the day, the performance of both cards is similar, however nvidia has killer features in the form of DLSS and much stronger RT support that make it objectively a better choice moving forward, whereas AMD offers little in return.

text:
So, RX 6000 results are in. Nice performing card to be honest!

The thing I'm confused about though, watching these reviews is this:

Vega64 $500, GTX1080 $600
Performance wise, they were pretty evenly matched, with Vega64 growing better with age than the 1080.
1080 is still widely regarded as epoch making and no real need to upgrade, Vega64 considered disappointing and you should sell it.

Radeon7 $700, RTX2080 $700
Performance wise, the Radeon7 usually performs better in games than the 2080, and with 16gb of HBM2 and a compute based architecture, performed much better in 3d production tasks. It has also aged better.
2080 was considered somewhat over priced and rarely got a solid recommendation, but Radeon7 was reported to be embarrassingly poor performing and you shouldn't touch it unless you specifically wanted the vRAM.

RX6800XT $650, RTX3080 $700
Performance wise, 6800XT trades blows and beats 3080, unless playing at 4k, where it is basically the same. 6800xt is lauded as exceptional and praise for AMD that they have finally brought the fight to nVidia with a genuinely competitive product, after the 3080 was 3 months ago declared surprisingly good and worth spending the money on for the value it offered, given how much of a performance uplift it provided over it's previous generation.

The competition in the graphics card sector hasn't actually moved. Basically not even at all. The only difference is that Vega was a year or so later than 1080, Radeon7 6 months or so later than 2080, and 6800XT 2 months later than 3080. But the actual value in the products doesn't change. So, why is the 6800XT so good, but the other cards got such bad reviews? I was expecting the 6800XT to actually consistently beat the 3080, because of how much of an apparently great product it is, but there's no difference in the competition?

Explain pls?

text: Thank you for focusing on 1440p testing as that is where most people are going to game with this generation of GPU.  4K performance is still low in some titles, and higher refresh monitors are still expensive for the titles that can run 120hz or so.  Some other reviewers seem to only be looking at 1080p and 4k because one shows CPU bottlenecked performance and the other shows fully GPU bottlenecked performance.  While this is the most efficient way to test and present both sides of the data set, the part lost in the middle is where most of us are going to find ourselves... The non-linear scaling of the Ampere GPUs is completely lost when you do it that way, and the 4K results make them look far more superior than they will really be for most gamers.  I mean, at 1440p the AMD GPU is pretty solidly in the lead in rasterization, which is still what most gamers care about.  So again, thank you for testing all 3 resolutions AND not giving DLSS and Ray Tracing  more weight than they deserve until they are valid features just as you say.  Only now are they somewhat viable and not just a marketing point for Nvidia.  It won't be until RDNA 3 and Hopper that it's really useful.

The AI part of DLSS is clearly fucking things up in many ways it shouldn't while the FSR 2.0 mod looks good even while moving around. Native rendering is far superior than both.

text:
Steve, your dismissal of RT performance seems a little bizarre to say the least, as is the omission of DLSS.  Sure, you might not personally feel that initial RTX implementations provided a meaningful enough visual return to warrant the frame-rate hit, but that same logic would apply equally to using Ultra settings that look nearly indistinguishable to high. Now that RT is being implemented more frequently in newer titles, playing with RT off is not actually playing at  "the highest quality settings" like it once was. RT isn't like the "hairworks" settings of old that were so marginal  they could safely be ignored (since most Nvidia users would ignore it as well).  In games like Metro Exodus, for example, ray-tracing makes a very real difference to the gameplay experience. It is far more impactful than switching between high and ultra presets. Watch Dogs Legion also looks meaningfully better with RT reflections than without. Odds are RT will become increasingly more important in upcoming titles like Cyberpunk 2077, so handwaving away its importance feels questionable. 

The same thing applies for DLSS. The vast majority of Geforce gamers playing Watch Dogs legion will be using DLSS if they are playing above 1080p. Not only was DLSS missing entirely from your comparison, you chose to spend a decent portion of the video highlighting a different "free performance boost" in a feature (SAM) that will only apply to the small niche of Ryzen 5000 owners. Why make a point of comparing the "improved" Radeon performance against the Nvidia cards if this competitive advantage will shortly disappear via a driver update anyway? 

There seems to be a double standard being applied here in regards to vendor-specific features that influence either visuals or performance. When these features favour Nvidia (RT titles, DLSS) they are either turned off or given a token 30 second segment. When these features favour AMD (SAM) they are highlighted.  Dismissing RT and DLSS made some sense in the early days of the RTX 2000 line, when the majority of gamers wouldn't utilize these features, barely any games offered the settings, and AMD cards didn't even support the feature. Now, it feels kind of partisan, especially considering you are already benching several  titles supporting one or both of these features. If Tim is recommending that people turn on DLSS and RT in Watch Dogs Legion, why are you presenting benchmarks with RT and DLSS both turned off?

text:
But you have to remember, Nvidia always has the follow up with their Ti and Super launches to fight back, AMD don't, or haven't in the last few generations.
If Nvidia do another Super launch, i.e. same price, more performance, the differences shown here will be even less, so it really will come down to preference at that point. Although at that point, because average performance differences are negligible, Nvidia will have the appeal of "superior real-time ray tracing" which will probably swing people to it, even though it's a pretty meaningless feature still, but, this worthless feature managed to pull people with the 20 series where it was worse, so I can see it happening again with the 30 series. Bearing in mind, price is no longer as big of an issue now with only a $50 difference. It's not like the 2070 Super vs 5700 XT, where it was a ridiculous $100+ difference, which was 20%+. $50 at $650 isn't even 8%, no one who can afford this is going to cry about. AMD has pretty much given up on the value proposition entirely now, as we've seen with the Ryzen 5000 and now the 6800 XT.

All I'm saying is, while the CPU launch was strong, it's too early to call the GPU a success. 5700 XT was the superior value but the market didn't accept it, and we might see that again with the 6800 XT as the value proposition is actually worse than the 5700 XT this time round.

text:
I feel AMD and Nvidia are in a really good position right now, performance wise.
We are comfortably in 4k gaming territory and no, 8k gaming won't be a thing ANYTIME soon.

So what I PERSONALLY would like to see for both of them to retain , or maybe slightly improve on raster performance, but dedicate future freed-up die space to RT and denoising hardware.
Especially AMD, since they will likely go to 5nm with RDNA3. I would love to see them leaving their rasterization portion of the die as is (in terms of rasterization perf.) and dedicate all leftover die space on RT/ML/DN cores and a bump in InfinityCache size, as I suspect Big Navi to choke on 4k assets that do not fit into the InfinityCache anymore.
There is no replacement for displacement- kinda thing. Ampere's higher VRAM bandwidth just overpowers AMDs workaround at 4k.

And they need a DLSS- competitor, like, yesterday.

Thoughts?

text:
It's great to see an AMD comeback, and it looks like that, if you are a gamers interested in games you can play RIGHT NOW, the 6800XT is the better choice, thanks to price/performance and power efficiency. And it may also have SLIGHTLY better availability.
That said, in general I think it's a different story, and the RX 6800XT is still not up there in terms of features.
If you are interested in ray tracing or future games (that may implement it more widely), it looks like the RTX 3080 is still the better option, although the higher quantity of VRAM may reveal useful in the future on the 6800XT...
If you not only game, but also stream, features like GeForce Now, RTX Voic, hardware encoders and other stuff like that make the RTX 3080 a way better product.
If you do rendering and you're actually interested in GPU acceleration, CUDA support is more widely spread and better utilised (in Windows! In Linux and MacOS your mileage may vary!).
And there's still the dark shadow of the RDNA 1 driver issues...
I hope they can sell many of these cards to actual gamers, so that gamers are happy with their purchase and AMD is able to earn enough money to spend on RND for the next generation of RDNA and more hardware/software features.
This RX 6800XT launch looks to me slightly worse than 1st generation Ryzen (also because they also had the potential for higher end cards with the 5700XT). I hope they can do incremental upgrades through drivers (so they can get enough to Ryzen 2000-like experience: refined Zen 1). But I'm mostly eager to see what they can get out of the RDNA 3... Zen 2-like improvements?

text: Average FPS across multiple games is a misleading metric! Games with more FPS will create bigger deltas in performance, and will carry more weight in the average. What we are actually wanting, is normalized averaged performance. For every game, mark the fastest card as 1x, and normalize others, then average that result. In that way, all games, regardless of the FPS count will carry the same weight. Please correct this for future reviews.

text:
@Dj-Mccullough  The comparison to the 5700xt is very flawed and extremely missleading. 5700xt had 40 CUs while the 6800 has 60CUs and the 6800xt 72 CUs. It is not like it was impossible for AMD to create 60CU or 72CU RDNA1 GPU, they just decided not to. So the gain from architecture to architecture will be much smaller when we are comparing 40 CU vs 40 CU (probably 6700 or 6700xt) and the difference between those 2 cards is the architectural gain. Probably more in line with 10-20% though both use the same node. RDNA3 will probably be on a better node so you will get some gains there aswell. 
But you will not see the same gains as when comparing 5700xt vs 6800xt. They will not produce 130-140CU gpus. Even their newly revealed MI100 data center chip only uses 128. So unless you want to pay 5000 bucks for a gaming gpu (and only leverage its performance at 8k) you will have to be satisfied with some architectural+node upgrades which probably will be more like 20-40% uplift.

author: @MLWJ1993

text:
No, memory is not the problem.  It's simply FP32 compute capacity.  The 6800 XT has 4608 FP32 ALU's.  The 3080 has 4352 dedicated FP32 ALU's, and another 4352 mixed-mode ALU's that can do FP32 when they're not doing INT32, in batches of 16.  In games at 4K, the 3080 is able to use about 30% of that extra FP32 capacity, meaning it has the practical equivalent of ~5600 FP32 Turing ALU's .  That's ~20% more usable FP32 ALU's than the 6800 XT at 4K, but the much higher clock speeds of the latter mean it only loses at 4K by about 5%.

A decently overclocked 6800 XT will probably make up that difference relatively easily, at the cost of power consumption, while the 3080 doesn't overclock well at all.

text:
@georges-leeeugene2905  Games focused on RT and DLSS, when those features are only in handful of games. DLSS is so overhyped that it makes me sick, you can get amazing screenshots, but on motion and on ray traced surfaces that scatter light (like the bronze doors on Control) it's noise hell that forced me to switch to lower native resolution.

To me having 16gb of VRAM is massively important. For those who upgrade every 1-2 years perhaps it's not, but having 8/10GB will lower the resell value when more games a starting to need above that amount of VRAM.

You are not going to get 3080 for 50 dollars more. That MSRP is the same BS than 2080ti's $999 was. Though we don't know what will happen to 6000 series, but I find it odd that we use MSRP as comparison, when it's totally obvious now that there wont be 3080s at that price coming probably ever. Even if it were just $50 dollars more, having 16Gb instead of 10GB makes 6800XT better value and compelling card, unless your use case specifically benefits from cuda or rtx broadcast.

Linus' attitude towards AMD GPUs has been quite horrible for a long time. With lots of erroneous claims. That came through from his video so clearly. FidelityFX also seems great at producing better quality graphics for no/minimal performance loss. Based on what I know about super resolution, it will become "plug and play" standard, if it really is going to be used by consoles too. And consoles having RDNA 2 ensures at least some advantages. And one thing also is that AMD's drivers usually get much better over time. 5700XT is prime example of that, now sitting clearly above 2070 Super.

While these are future promises, on review about "compelling card" these matter a ton. And I think the real price difference between 6800XT and 3080 will stay quite big. If Nvidia manages to get cards close to MSRP, I would guess AMD lowers their prices to keep that price advantage. Though 6800 at it's price point is not nearly as compelling. But essentially it's just 6800XT with 12 CUs disabled, lower clocks are for TDP marketing purposes, that should overclock like crazy.

text: @choatus  The basis of my argument is that the Nvidia cards only exceed the AMD card's performance in 4k, so their best use case is for 4k gaming, but the limited Vram might make that a moot point in the next cycle of games (without turning down settings.) Microsoft Flight Sim already allocates over 17Gb of Vram in 4k when under high load and nearly 10Gb in 1440p. Actual usage seems to be around 12Gb/8Gb respectively.  The new trend in game development is to early access release games with shit optimization, and the optimization never seems to get addressed even at final release.  AAA titles like COD that release every year are the same in a lot of ways. I think Warzone will use over 8Gb.  It seems like Nvidia kept the Vram low because GDDR6X is expensive, but it keeps the 3070/3080 from being "Great" 4k cards for the future.  They could have achieved the same memory bandwidth with more slower GDDR6 for roughly the same cost.
author: @Vlalada0

text: @Vlalada0  to achieve the same bandwidth as GDDR6x they need to have 3-4 times the amount of normal GDDR6 so no it doesnt work like that.. it would end up costing a ton more to do it that way for starters. P.s MSFS on my 3080 in 4k uses (not allocates) less than 7gb of vram right now in ultra. but that game is broken as it needs its update to DX12 before we can see what it really runs like, it's basically running on 2 cores only atm.

author: @bastordd

text:
@legendarymop  The cpu bottleneck is working against AMD not nvidia.

The reason that Nvidia has more performance at 4k is because of the FP32 compute (tons of cores) which doesn't scale well at lower resolution.

There is a CPU bottleneck at 1080p and a little one at 1440p, but it bottlenecks RDNA 2 more than Nvidia.

The rtx3090 is only slightly more powerful than a 3080 and runs at similar clocks, it's an architecture bottleneck at lower resolutions for the RTX3000 series.

So for fps snobs at lower resolutions it's RDNA 2 all the way now. (Massive 40%+ performance difference in some games)

For 4K snobs it's slightly more in favor of Nvidia. (18-20%+  performance difference in some games)

text:
@Animik.Rahman.9  Why do you think that 4K would reveal a memory bandwidth bottleneck?

Steve has explained the reason why the Ampere cards do so well at 4K compared to lower resolutions. It has to do with the doubled floating point units in the Ampere architecture. In lower resolutions, the other areas in the GPU become the bottleneck as they cannot feed the many floating point units with enough data to take advantage of them. But for 4K and beyond, this is not such a problem any longer, and the Ampere architecture can better utilize its many floating point units.

Steve made a video about it right after the initial RTX 3000 launch comparing the 3080 to the 2080Ti at resolution scaling: https://youtu.be/c7npXXyXJzI

Steve's conclusion with 14 games was that the 2080Ti allowed for an average of 83 fps at 2160p, with 1440p performance being 77% higher at 147 fps. The 3080 allowed for 108 at 2160p, with 1440p performance being just 68% higher at 181 fps.

You can make the same kind of comparison using the data from the 18 games used in this video. At 1440p, the 3080 delivers 153 fps on average, which is 56% higher than the 2160p performance at 98 fps. Do the same for the 6800XT, and the performance difference grows to 71%. For this data, the performance difference of the 2080Ti sits at 69%. The outlier in this case is the 3080, not the 6800XT.

If you think the problem is the lower memory bandwidth, then take a look at the Radeon VII, which is anything but bandwidth starved because of its overkill HBM2 memory giving it 1028 GB/s bandwidth. It offers 76% higher performance at 1440p over 2160p. Even more than the 6800XT and 2080Ti.

The extreme outlier is still the big Ampere cards. The 6800XT is not bandwidth starved. Its the Ampere cards that cannot take advantage of their large floating point units in resolutions below 2160p.
